body:
Two changes to `BatchedTridiagonalSolver`. Both leave results bitwise unchanged.

**1. Carry the Thomas sweep in registers (always on).** Each column is swept by one thread, so the solve time is the length of the level-to-level dependency chain. The pivot β, the elimination ratio tᵏ, and the solution of the level just solved are now carried in local variables instead of being read back from `t` and `ϕ` right after they are stored. The compiler can't do this itself because it can't prove `ϕ` and `t` don't alias the coefficients. Carried values are converted to the stored array's element type, so results are unchanged. The x, y and z sweeps now share one kernel body (`column_index` maps a level to `(i, j, k)`).

**2. Optional stored factorization.** A new keyword, `factorized = false` by default, which keeps the current behavior. With `factorized = true` the solver stores the factorization of its systems, which depends only on the coefficients, not on the right-hand side:

```
β¹ = b¹,    βᵏ = bᵏ − aᵏ⁻¹ tᵏ,    tᵏ = cᵏ⁻¹ / βᵏ⁻¹,    k = 2, …, N
```

```julia
solver = BatchedTridiagonalSolver(grid; lower_diagonal, diagonal, upper_diagonal, factorized = true)
compute_factorization!(solver, args...)   # whenever the coefficients change
solve!(ϕ, solver, rhs, args...)           # many times: substitution only
```

- `compute_factorization!` evaluates the coefficients once and stores β and `a` (a `TridiagonalFactors`). The ratios `t` stay in the solver's existing scratch array.
- A factorized `solve!` evaluates neither the coefficients nor the recurrence, and reads only the right-hand side per level.
- This is for systems solved many times with unchanged coefficients and different right-hand sides, such as the vertical solves of a compressible model's acoustic substep loop, which are fixed within a Runge-Kutta stage.
- The caller calls `compute_factorization!` again whenever the coefficients change, including through `args`. A factorized `solve!` does not detect changed coefficients. `compute_factorization!` on an unfactorized solver throws an `ArgumentError`.
- The factorization uses the same floating-point operations as the unfactored sweep. Tests check bitwise equality for x, y and z, for several right-hand sides per factorization, in place, and after refactoring with changed coefficients.

### Benchmarks

Whole step, `HydrostaticFreeSurfaceModel` with CATKE (vertically implicit), 256³, Δt = 60 s (ms/step, two runs; tridiagonal-solve time in parentheses):

| GPU | FT | main | register sweep | change |
|-|-|-|-|-|
| H100 | F32 | 9.33 (2.65) | 8.98 (2.29) | −3.7 % |
| H100 | F64 | 11.84 (3.50) | 11.44 (3.09) | −3.4 % |
| A100 | F32 | 16.0–16.3 (4.0–4.4) | 15.3–15.6 (3.26) | −4.2 % |
| A100 | F64 | 20.7–20.9 (5.24) | 20.3–20.5 (4.83) | −2.0 % |

The register sweep gains more inside the model, where coefficients are computed in the sweep. Results are bitwise identical to main (solver and 10 model steps: u, v, w, T, S, e).

The stored factorization pays off when one factorization serves many solves. It is not benchmarked here in isolation; in Breeze's acoustic substep loop, factoring once per stage and substituting per substep was part of a 10–12 % reduction in ms/step (NumericalEarth/Breeze.jl#1242, which now uses this API). An earlier pivots-only version of change 2 gave no measurable gain for the solver alone (A100, up to 512²×256), because it still evaluated `a` and `c` in every solve.

Related: NumericalEarth/Breeze.jl#1242 replaces its own stored tridiagonal factors with this. #6478 (pentadiagonal solver with a factor-once / substitute-many API) will be updated to follow the same interface (`factorized`, `compute_factorization!`, one `solve!`).
